title: Backtracking
tagline: Systematically explore all candidate solutions by building them incrementally and abandoning ('pruning') any path that cannot lead to a valid answer.

sections.content:
Backtracking is a **refined brute-force** algorithm design technique. It builds a solution one choice at a time, forming a **decision tree** where each node represents a partial candidate and each branch represents a choice. When a partial candidate violates a constraint — meaning it can never be extended to a valid solution — the algorithm **prunes** that branch and backtracks to the previous choice point, trying the next option. This avoids the pure brute-force explosion of enumerating all possible combinations upfront.

Backtracking is the right tool when the problem requires **exploring a combinatorial search space** subject to constraints: N-queens (place n queens on an n×n board with no conflicts), permutations and subsets, sudoku, graph colouring, word search, and constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). The worst case is still exponential — pruning does not change the theoretical bound — but in practice backtracking explores a tiny fraction of the search space, making it tractable for moderate n.

sections.title: Solving a Maze by Marking Dead Ends
sections.content:
Imagine navigating a maze. A pure brute-force approach would enumerate every possible path from start to finish — exponentially many. A smarter strategy: walk until you hit a dead end or revisit a cell, then retreat to the last junction and try the next untried direction. Mark dead ends so you never walk them again.

This is backtracking: you build a path incrementally (choice by choice), check after each step whether you are still on a valid trajectory (no dead end, no cycle), and backtrack when you are not. The maze constraint prunes entire subtrees of the decision tree — a dead-end passage eliminates all paths that include it. For well-constrained problems (dense constraint satisfaction), the pruning can be dramatic — the effective search tree is orders of magnitude smaller than the theoretical worst case.

**The backtracking template** follows a universal recursive structure: (1) check if the current partial solution satisfies the goal — if yes, record it; (2) check if the current state violates a constraint — if yes, return immediately (prune); (3) otherwise, for each available choice, make the choice, recurse, then **undo** the choice (backtrack). The undo step is critical — it restores state so the next sibling branch sees a clean slate.

**N-Queens** illustrates the template clearly. Place queens one per row; for each row, try each column. Before placing, check if the column or either diagonal is already attacked. If attacked, skip this column (prune). If n queens are placed without conflicts, record the solution. The constraint check eliminates entire subtrees: for n=8, there are 8^8 = 16 million brute-force placements but only 92 valid solutions — backtracking finds them by exploring roughly 15,000 nodes rather than 16 million.

**Permutations** use backtracking with a 'used' set: for each position in the output, choose any unused element, mark it used, recurse on the remaining positions, then unmark it. This generates all n! permutations. **Subsets** (power set) use a binary choice at each element: include or exclude. With n elements, this produces 2^n subsets, which is exactly the number of leaf nodes — but the decision tree of depth n with branching factor 2 is far more structured than a flat loop over all bitmasks.

**Pruning strategies** separate efficient backtracking from naive enumeration. For sudoku, constraint propagation (after placing a digit, eliminate it from all peers in the same row, column, and 3×3 box) can solve many cells without backtracking. Choosing the most-constrained variable first (minimum remaining values heuristic) ensures backtracking happens early and high in the tree — maximising pruning impact.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: N-Queens uses three sets to track attacked columns and diagonals — O(1) constraint check per cell. The constraint check (pruning) before each recursive call is what makes backtracking efficient: rows where every column is attacked return immediately without deeper recursion. permutations uses a boolean 'used' array for O(1) include/exclude. Both follow the identical template: choose → recurse → unchoose.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Prune early and high in the tree.** The most impactful pruning happens at the top of the decision tree — a cut at depth 1 eliminates an entire subtree of depth n-1. Two strategies: (1) **Constraint check before recursing** — check validity before the recursive call rather than at the start of the call; this avoids even entering invalid subtrees. (2) **Most-constrained variable first** — in CSPs like sudoku, pick the cell with the fewest valid digits next; if a cell has only one valid digit, it must be that — committing early eliminates branches globally. These heuristics can reduce practical running time by orders of magnitude while leaving the worst-case bound unchanged.

items: Backtracking is **constrained exhaustive search**: build the solution incrementally, **prune** any partial candidate that violates a constraint, and **undo** each choice before trying the next — the undo (backtrack) step is essential to restore state.
The **universal template** is: if goal reached → record; if invalid → prune (return); else for each choice → make choice → recurse → undo choice.
**N-Queens** uses three constraint sets (columns, two diagonals) checked in O(1) per cell — pruning reduces 8^8 ≈ 16M brute-force positions to ~15k explored nodes for n=8.
**Subsets** use include/exclude branching at each element (2^n leaves); **permutations** use a 'used' set and branch on unused elements (n! leaves) — both follow the identical backtracking template.
**Pruning effectiveness** determines practical performance: prune early (before recursing), and use domain heuristics (most-constrained variable first) to maximise the subtrees eliminated per check.

quiz.question: What distinguishes backtracking from plain brute-force enumeration?
options: Backtracking uses dynamic programming to cache partial solutions
Backtracking prunes branches that violate constraints, avoiding full enumeration of invalid subtrees
Backtracking always runs in polynomial time; brute-force is exponential
Backtracking only works on sorted input
quiz.explanation: Brute-force generates all candidates and filters. Backtracking builds candidates incrementally and prunes (abandons) any partial candidate the moment it violates a constraint — entire subtrees are skipped without enumeration. In practice this can reduce explored states by orders of magnitude, though worst-case is still exponential.

quiz.question: In the backtracking template, what is the purpose of the 'undo' (backtrack) step?
options: It deletes the solution found in this branch to save memory
It restores the state to what it was before the current choice, so the next sibling choice sees a clean slate
It signals the recursion to terminate when no valid solutions exist
It re-sorts the available choices before trying the next option
quiz.explanation: Because backtracking uses a single mutable state (board, path, used-set), each recursive call must restore the state it modified before returning — otherwise the next sibling branch inherits incorrect state. The undo step makes the state changes reversible, enabling the exploration of all branches from a clean starting point.

quiz.question: How many valid solutions does the 8-Queens problem have?
quiz.explanation: There are exactly 92 distinct solutions to the 8-Queens problem (placing 8 queens on an 8×8 chessboard with no two queens attacking each other). Of these, 12 are fundamentally distinct solutions (not related by rotation or reflection). The brute-force search space is 8^8 ≈ 16 million; backtracking with constraint pruning explores only ~15,720 nodes.

quiz.question: In N-Queens, what three constraint sets are tracked to detect conflicts in O(1) per cell?
options: Rows, columns, and cells
Columns, \ diagonals (row-col), and / diagonals (row+col)
Upper-left, upper-right, and center regions
Horizontal bands, vertical bands, and corners
quiz.explanation: A queen at (row, col) attacks its entire column, its \ diagonal (all cells where row-col is constant), and its / diagonal (all cells where row+col is constant). Storing three sets keyed on col, (row-col), and (row+col) enables O(1) conflict detection for any candidate cell, versus O(n) scanning.

quiz.question: How many subsets does backtracking generate for an array of n distinct elements?
options: n!
n²
quiz.explanation: Each element has exactly two choices: include or exclude. With n elements and independent binary choices, there are 2^n possible subsets (the power set). The backtracking decision tree has depth n and branching factor 2, producing exactly 2^n leaf nodes, each corresponding to a unique subset.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of generating all permutations of n distinct elements via backtracking?
options: O(n²)
O(n log n)
O(n! * n)
quiz.explanation: There are n! permutations, and copying each complete permutation to the result takes O(n). The total work for generating and recording all permutations is O(n! · n). The recursion tree has n! leaves at depth n, with branching factor decreasing from n at depth 0 to 1 at depth n-1 — total nodes = sum_{k=0}^{n} n!/k! which is O(n! · e) ≈ O(n!).

quiz.question: In the subset generation backtracking, why does the `start` parameter increase with each recursive call?
options: To prevent memory overflow by limiting recursion depth
To avoid including the same element twice — only elements at index >= start are candidates for the current position
To sort the subsets in lexicographic order
To skip elements that have already been pruned
quiz.explanation: Passing `start = i + 1` to the recursive call ensures each subsequent element in the path has a higher index than the previous one. This generates each unique subset exactly once (in order), and avoids both duplicate subsets and including the same element twice. Without this, [1,2] and [2,1] would both appear.

quiz.question: Why does placing the pruning check BEFORE the recursive call (rather than at the start of each call) improve performance?
options: It reduces the number of sets that need to be maintained
It avoids the function call overhead for invalid branches — the subtree is pruned without even entering the recursive call
It enables memoization of pruned branches
It converts the algorithm from O(n!) to O(n²)
quiz.explanation: Every function call has overhead (stack frame allocation, argument passing). If the constraint check is inside the called function, an invalid branch still incurs a function call before returning. Checking before the call eliminates that overhead entirely — no stack frame is created for invalid branches. More importantly, it also prunes children of the invalid state without recursing into them.

quiz.question: The 'most-constrained variable' heuristic in sudoku backtracking means:
options: Always fill cells in row-major order (top-left to bottom-right)
Choose the empty cell with the fewest valid digit options next — so failures are detected earliest
Fill cells with the most neighbours first
Always try digit 1 before digit 2 before digit 3, and so on
quiz.explanation: The minimum remaining values (MRV) heuristic selects the most-constrained empty cell — the one with the fewest valid digits. A cell with only 1 valid digit must be that digit (commit for free). A cell with 2 options fails 50% of the time immediately, pruning the tree high. This front-loads failures, maximising the size of subtrees eliminated per backtrack.

quiz.question: Backtracking is best categorised as which type of algorithm?
options: A greedy algorithm — it commits to the locally best choice at each step
A dynamic programming algorithm — it caches subproblem solutions to avoid recomputation
A constrained exhaustive search — it explores all candidates but prunes invalid subtrees early
A divide-and-conquer algorithm — it splits the search space into independent halves
quiz.explanation: Backtracking is constrained exhaustive search — it does not commit greedily (it can backtrack), does not cache subproblem results (no memoisation), and does not divide into independent halves (branches share state). The key characteristic is constraint-based pruning of the search tree during incremental construction of candidates.
